title: The Official Scoreboard
part: PART ONE: EIGHT GAMES, ZERO WINS

pages.text:
*Way to Lose #1: Show up.*

Here is the official scoreboard of my soccer career so far. Games played: 7. Games won: 0. Goals we have let in: 43. That works out to six and a bit goals per game, which sounds like a lot until you see our goalkeeper, Priya, who is terrified of the ball, standing in front of the net like a small brave umbrella in a hailstorm.

I am the captain. Nobody voted. It just kind of happened, the way a bruise happens.

My name is Dani Ruiz, I am twelve, and I play central midfield for the Marigold Park Mud Hens, which is the worst under-13 team in the entire Harbor Valley Youth League. I know because I checked. I checked the standings on the league website every morning before school, the way some people check their own pulse, and every morning we were at the bottom, right underneath a team called the Sunnyvale Sprouts, who have never once been sunny.
pages.image: Dani, a wiry 12-year-old girl with brown skin, a high dark ponytail with a yellow elastic and a yellow captain's armband, stands alone on a muddy soccer field holding a soccer ball under one arm and looking up at a big scoreboard with only small round lights showing 0 goals for her side and many for the other; a duck pond behind the goal.

pages.text:
Here is our field. Marigold Park has one soccer pitch, and it slants to the left, so every ball you kick eventually rolls toward the parking lot like it has somewhere better to be. Behind the west goal there is a duck pond. The ducks have opinions. Twice this season a shot has gone over the crossbar and into the water, and both times a duck picked up the ball, looked me in the eye, and refused to give it back.

Here is my team. In goal: Priya Nair, eleven, tiny, glasses strapped to her head with a sports band, gloves as big as boxing mitts. At defense: Tank Bell, who is twelve and the size of a refrigerator and apologizes to every player he tackles, and the Cruz twins, Leo and Mateo, who finish each other's sentences and argue all game about which of them is older. On the wing: Josie Kaplan, who has never stopped talking in her life. Up front: Ahmed Suleiman, the fastest kid in the league, who believes that passing is for people who are slow.

And on the bench, holding a bag of orange slices and smiling like it's his birthday: Ollie Pratt, who has played eleven minutes all year.
pages.image: The team lines up on a muddy slanted soccer field before a game in red jerseys: tiny Priya with oversized gloves, huge gentle Tank, two identical boys, a talkative girl with wild curly hair, a lanky fast boy, and a cheerful boy on the bench holding a bag of orange slices; a duck stands near the pond behind them.

pages.text:
Game eight is against the Hollis Hornets, who are not even a good team, and by the ninth minute it is 3 to 0.

Let me describe how a goal against us usually goes, for those of you who are lucky enough not to know. First, the other team does something perfectly normal, like passing to each other. Then Ahmed, who was supposed to be tracking back, is standing at midfield admiring his shoelaces. Then the twins both go for the same ball and bump into each other, and Tank says, "Sorry, sorry, sorry," to nobody in particular. Then there is a very small, very quiet *pfft* as the ball goes past Priya, who has closed her eyes.

"And Ruiz has the ball," I say, in my head, in my announcer voice, the voice I use when things are going badly. "She's looking left. She's looking right. She's looking for a way out of this entire situation."

There is no way out. There is only forward.
pages.image: Mid-game on a muddy field, Priya in goal has her eyes squeezed shut as a ball flies past her into the net; Tank in front of her is apologizing with hands raised, the twins have bumped into each other, and Ahmed stands far away at midfield looking at his shoes; Dani runs in the middle with a frustrated face.

pages.text:
On the sideline, my family is doing what they do best, which is being loud. My dad, who fixes school buses at the depot and wears a foam finger to every game, is holding the finger high above his head and yelling, "Come on, Mud Hens! That's all right! That's okay! Shake it off!" He has yelled this exact sentence eight games in a row. It has never once worked.

My abuela sits beside him in her folding chair with her arms crossed. She still does not understand offside. She thinks it is a kind of rude behavior. "Why is that boy allowed to stand there and you are not?" she asks my little sister, Luz, who is seven and busy writing in a crayon notebook. Luz calls it the Deputy Loss Log. She is thorough. She writes "GOAL" in big red letters every time it happens and draws a very sad duck.

With four minutes left it is 7 to 0. I get the ball at midfield. I see a gap. I take off.

And then, the way you can see your own shoe coming before you trip on it, I watch myself do it. I turn to pass back to Priya, so she at least has something to do, and I hit it a little too well.
pages.image: Dani sprints through the middle of a muddy soccer field with a determined face; on the sideline, a big loud dad in a mechanic's shirt waves a foam finger, a small sharp-eyed grandmother in a cardigan sits with arms crossed, and a little girl with pigtails writes in a crayon notebook.

pages.text:
It goes straight past Priya. Straight into the net. Our net.

The whole park goes quiet. Even the ducks look up.

"Own goal," says the ref, kindly, in the voice you'd use to tell a person they had spinach in their teeth.

I stand there with my hands on my head. Eight to nothing, and all of it, I feel, is somehow my personal fault. Forty-three plus eight is fifty-one. I do the math right there on the field, because I can't help it. Tank comes over to pat my shoulder and says, "Sorry, Dani," which is the worst part, because it wasn't even his fault to begin with.

Then, when I look up, I see a boy from my school on the bleachers behind the goal. His name is Carter Boyle. He is holding up his phone. It is pointed straight at me, and the little red light on it is on.

I do the only thing a captain can do. I pick the ball out of the net, I tuck it under my arm, and I say to it, very clearly, "I'm sorry."
pages.image: Dani stands in front of her own net with hands on her head and a soccer ball in the net behind her, looking up in dismay at a boy on the bleachers holding up a phone to film her; Tank pats her shoulder apologetically; the ref stands nearby.
